claim: In area CA1 of the hippocampus, the selection of place cells to represent a new environment is biased towards neurons with higher excitability.
source: In area CA1 of the hippocampus, the selection of place cells to represent a new environment is biased towards neurons with higher excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Different environments are represented by orthogonal cell ensembles in CA1.
source: However, different environments are represented by orthogonal cell ensembles, suggesting that regulatory mechanisms exist.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations.

claim: Theta-bursts of action potentials induce a long-lasting, homeostatic depression of intrinsic excitability in CA1 pyramidal neurons in vivo.
source: We observed a long-lasting, homeostatic depression of intrinsic excitability which commenced within minutes
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings.

claim: The homeostatic depression of intrinsic excitability in CA1 pyramidal neurons in vivo is not mediated by dendritic Ih.
source: and, in contrast to in vitro observations, was not mediated by dendritic Ih.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that blocking Ih did not prevent the plasticity.

claim: The homeostatic depression of intrinsic excitability is attenuated by the Kv1.1 channel blocker dendrotoxin K.
source: Instead, it was attenuated by the Kv1.1 channel blocker dendrotoxin K, suggesting an axonal origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using DTX-K.

claim: Place cells show an experience-dependent reduction in out-of-field firing consistent with decreased excitability.
source: Analysis of place cells' out-of-field firing in mice navigating in virtual reality further revealed an experience-dependent reduction consistent with decreased excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of extracellular recording data from mice in virtual reality.

claim: The recruitment of cells to represent any new association or environment is biased towards those cells with high levels of intrinsic excitability in the amygdala and hippocampus.
source: In the amygdala and hippocampus it has been shown that the recruitment of cells to represent any new association or environment is biased towards those cells with high levels of intrinsic excitability (Yiu et al., 2014; Pignatelli et al., 2019; Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016; Alme et al., 2014; Rich et al., 2014; Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014; Han et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2009; Epsztein et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Higher excitability correlates with CA1 pyramidal neurons becoming place cells in a novel environment.
source: In particular, intracellular recordings from individual CA1 pyramidal neurons have shown that higher excitability correlates with neurons becoming place cells in a novel environment (Epsztein et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Enhancing excitability with depolarizations of just a few millivolts is sufficient to reveal place specific activity in previously silent CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: and that enhancing excitability with depolarizations of just a few millivolts is sufficient to reveal place specific activity in previously silent cells (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The populations representing different environments are largely orthogonal.
source: However, given that the populations representing different environments are largely orthogonal (Leutgeb et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2005), a regulatory mechanism is needed to diversify recruitment and prevent the same cells from always being activated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurons can adapt their excitability to maintain their activity within set bounds.
source: One attractive mechanism is homeostatic regulation of intrinsic excitability based on firing rate history, as it is known that neurons can adapt their excitability to maintain their activity within set bounds (Turrigiano et al., 1994; Desai et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: High frequency bursts of action potentials alone can induce a homeostatic decrease in the global excitability of CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Some studies have shown, however, that high frequency bursts of action potentials alone can induce a homeostatic decrease in the global excitability of CA1 pyramidal neurons (Fan et al., 2005; Narayanan and Johnston, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: The in vitro plasticity of CA1 pyramidal neuron excitability was mediated by an upregulation of the hyperpolarization-activated cation current (Ih).
source: However, this plasticity was mediated by an upregulation of the hyperpolarization-activated cation current (Ih)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: Ih is primarily expressed in the dendrites where it strongly influences synaptic integration.
source: and it is thus questionable whether it would serve this function under natural conditions, as Ih is primarily expressed in the dendrites where it strongly influences synaptic integration (Magee, 1998; Tsay et al., 2007) and plasticity (Maroso et al., 2016; Nolan et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Stimulations inducing weaker, more physiological, levels of synaptic potentiation can locally reduce Ih and enhance dendritic excitability around potentiated synapses.
source: Stimulations inducing weaker, more physiological, levels of synaptic potentiation can also have the opposite effect, locally reducing Ih and enhancing dendritic excitability around potentiated synapses (Campanac et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were obtained from 56 CA1 pyramidal neurons in anesthetized rats.
source: We obtained whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from CA1 pyramidal neurons (n = 56) in anesthetized rats using the blind technique (Lee et al., 2009; Margrie et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods described.

claim: The identity of the recorded cell was verified in 45 out of 56 cases by biocytin staining.
source: The identity of the cell was verified in 45 out of 56 cases by biocytin staining (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Following TBS, there was a long-lasting reduction in intrinsic excitability that began within minutes of the stimulation.
source: Following TBS we saw a long-lasting reduction in intrinsic excitability that began within minutes of the stimulation (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Average firing rates were significantly reduced 20 min post-TBS (Change in firing rate: TBS −29.2 ± 7.1%, p=7.3×10−4, n = 16).
source: Average firing rates were significantly reduced 20 min post-TBS (Change in firing rate: TBS −29.2 ± 7.1%, p=7.3×10−4, n = 16, Figure 1E)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Control cells did not show a significant reduction in firing rate (−5.3 ± 4.8%, p=0.20, n = 11).
source: which was not seen in control cells (−5.3 ± 4.8%, p=0.20, n = 11, Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The magnitude of the reduction in excitability correlated with the number of spikes evoked during the TBS (R2 = 0.40, p=0.0083).
source: The magnitude of the reduction correlated with the number of spikes evoked during the TBS (R2 = 0.40, p=0.0083; Figure 1G) in line with a homeostatic mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The reduction in firing rate after TBS was uniform across all current step amplitudes, resulting in a rightward shift in the input/output curve with no change in the slope.
source: We found that the reduction in firing rate after TBS was uniform across all current step amplitudes, resulting in a rightward shift in the input/output curve with no change in the slope of the fits (Slope: Pre vs 10 min p=0.78, 20 min p=0.34 and 30 min p=0.43, Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The current threshold was significantly increased by the TBS protocol (Intercept: Pre vs 10 min p=0.044, n = 16, 20 min p=0.024, n = 16, 30 min p=0.28 n=14).
source: As a result the current threshold was significantly increased by the TBS protocol (Intercept: Pre vs 10 min p=0.044, n = 16, 20 min p=0.024, n = 16, 30 min p=0.28 n=14).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: No effect on slope or intercept was seen in control cells (Pre vs 10 min p=0.26, n = 11, 20 min p=0.49, n = 11, 30 min p=0.27, n = 6).
source: No effect on slope or intercept was seen in control cells (Pre vs 10 min p=0.26, n = 11, 20 min p=0.49, n = 11, 30 min p=0.27, n = 6, Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The change in firing rate did not show any relationship with the initial input resistance (R2 = 0.11, p=0.21).
source: The effect of TBS did not appear to relate to the initial excitability state of the cell, as the change in firing rate did not show any relationship with the initial input resistance (R2 = 0.11, p=0.21, F Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The change in firing rate did not show any relationship with the initial membrane potential (R2 = 0.015, p=0.66).
source: membrane potential (R2 = 0.015, p=0.66, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The change in firing rate did not show any relationship with the initial action potential threshold (R2 = 0.0045, p=0.80).
source: action potential threshold (R2 = 0.0045, p=0.80, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The change in firing rate did not show any relationship with the initial burstiness (R2 = 0.02, p=0.60).
source: or burstiness (R2 = 0.02, p=0.60, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: A short episode of theta-burst firing is sufficient to induce a fast and long-lasting decrease in intrinsic excitability of CA1 pyramidal cells in vivo.
source: Our results therefore show that a short episode of theta-burst firing is sufficient to induce a fast and long-lasting decrease in intrinsic excitability of CA1 pyramidal cells in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: There was a reduction in the input resistance following TBS that correlated well with the reduction in excitability (pre vs 20 min p=0.0087, n = 16; R2 = 0.38, p=0.012).
source: We found a reduction in the input resistance following TBS that correlated well with the reduction in excitability (pre vs 20 min p=0.0087, n = 16; R2 = 0.38, p=0.012, Figure 2A–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The reduction in input resistance was significant compared to control cells (Change in Rin: TBS −9.7 ± 2.6%, n = 16, Control −1.8 ± 2.5%, n = 11, p=0.043).
source: and that was significant compared to control cells (Change in Rin: TBS −9.7 ± 2.6%, n = 16, Control −1.8 ± 2.5%, n = 11, p=0.043, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: There was an increase in the latency to first spike that correlated with the change in excitability (pre vs 20 min p=0.005, n = 16; R2 = 0.69, p=1.6×10−4).
source: We similarly found an increase in the latency to first spike that correlated with the change in excitability (pre vs 20 min p=0.005, n = 16; R2 = 0.69, p=1.6×10−4, Figure 2E–G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in latency to first spike was significant compared to control (Change in latency: TBS 103.4 ± 29.5%, n = 16, Control 19.6 ± 12.8%, n = 11, p=0.034).
source: and that was significant compared to control (Change in latency: TBS 103.4 ± 29.5%, n = 16, Control 19.6 ± 12.8%, n = 11, p=0.034, Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Sub-threshold conductances might be modified by the TBS protocol.
source: These observations suggest that sub-threshold conductances might be modified by the TBS protocol.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed changes in input resistance and latency to first spike.

claim: There was no difference in membrane potential variance before versus 20 min post-TBS (pre vs 20 min p=0.84, n = 16).
source: There was no difference in variance before versus 20 min post-TBS (pre vs 20 min p=0.84, n = 16, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no correlation between membrane potential variance change and the change in excitability (R2 = 0.03 p=0.53).
source: no correlation with the change in excitability (R2 = 0.03 p=0.53, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no difference in membrane potential variance compared to control cells (∆Variance: TBS −0.03 ± 0.16 mV2 n=16, Control 0.39 ± 0.22 mV2, n = 11, p=0.12).
source: or difference compared to control cells (∆Variance: TBS −0.03 ± 0.16 mV2 n=16, Control 0.39 ± 0.22 mV2, n = 11, p=0.12, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: After TBS there was an increase in the action potential threshold (pre vs 20 min p<0.019, n = 16).
source: Although after TBS there was an increase in the action potential threshold (pre vs 20 min p<0.019, n = 16, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The difference in action potential threshold between control and TBS cells was not significant (∆Threshold: TBS 1.16 ± 0.44 mV, n = 16, Control 0.44 ± 0.54 mV, n = 10, p=0.32).
source: the difference between control and TBS cells was not significant (∆Threshold: TBS 1.16 ± 0.44 mV, n = 16, Control 0.44 ± 0.54 mV, n = 10, p=0.32, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no effect of TBS on the AHP (pre vs 20 min p=0.92, ∆AHP: TBS 0.4 ± 0.48 mV, n = 16, Control −0.48 ± 0.37 mV, p=0.19, n = 11).
source: We did not find any effect on the AHP (pre vs 20 min p=0.92, ∆AHP: TBS 0.4 ± 0.48 mV, n = 16, Control −0.48 ± 0.37 mV, p=0.19, n = 11, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Changes in supra-threshold conductances are unlikely to explain the decrease in excitability observed.
source: These observations indicate that changes in supra-threshold conductances are unlikely to explain the decrease in excitability we observed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of significant changes in action potential threshold and AHP.

claim: In the presence of BAPTA (0.5 mM), the depression of intrinsic excitability was prevented (BAPTA n = 7, change in firing rate: 23.0 ± 13.7%, p=0.0012 vs TBS).
source: As expected, in the presence of BAPTA the depression of intrinsic excitability was prevented (BAPTA n = 7, change in firing rate: 23.0 ± 13.7%, p=0.0012 vs TBS; change in Rin: 2.4% ± 5.16, p=0.029 vs TBS; change in latency: 8.7 ± 7.4%, p=0.05 vs TBS, Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Blocking NMDARs by adding 1 mM MK-801 to intracellular solution did not affect the TBS-induced reduction in excitability (MK-801 n = 7, change in firing rate: −42.1 ± 12.2%, p=0.35 vs TBS).
source: We found, however, that blocking NMDARs by adding 1 mM MK-801 to intracellular solution did not affect the TBS-induced reduction in excitability (MK-801 n = 7, change in firing rate: −42.1 ± 12.2%, p=0.35 vs TBS; change in Rin: −13.2 ± 2.5%, p=0.43 vs TBS; change in latency: 156.4 ± 70.3%, p=0.42 vs TBS, Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Influx through voltage-gated calcium channels is the major, or at least initial, source of calcium for the induction of the plasticity observed.
source: This is perhaps unsurprising given the lack of potentiating synaptic stimulation, and we can infer that influx through voltage-gated calcium channels is the major, or at least initial, source of calcium for the induction of the plasticity we observed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the fact that BAPTA blocked the plasticity but MK-801 did not.

claim: The sag ratio actually increased following TBS (pre vs 20 min p=0.0088, n = 16).
source: However, we found that the sag ratio actually increased following TBS (pre vs 20 min p=0.0088, n = 16, Figure 5B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in sag ratio indicates a decrease in Ih that would be expected to make the cells more excitable.
source: which indicates a decrease in Ih that would be expected to make the cells more excitable.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the relationship between sag ratio and Ih.

claim: The decrease in sag ratio was not detected in the presence of BAPTA and MK-801 (BAPTA p=0.39, n = 7, MK-801 p=0.97, n = 7).
source: This decrease was not detected in the presence of BAPTA and MK-801 (BAPTA p=0.39, n = 7, MK-801 p=0.97, n = 7, Figure 5C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The change in sag ratio was inversely correlated with the strength of stimulation (R2 = 0.42, p=0.0065).
source: The change in sag ratio was inversely correlated with the strength of stimulation (R2 = 0.42, p=0.0065, Figure 5D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The change in sag ratio did not significantly correlate with the overall change in excitability (R2 = 0.08, p=0.29).
source: but did not significantly correlate with the overall change in excitability (R2 = 0.08, p=0.29, Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Intracellular ZD7288 did not prevent TBS-induced decrease in firing rate (ZD n = 6, change in firing rate: −22.9 ± 8.6%, p=0.63 vs TBS).
source: However, intracellular ZD7288 did not prevent TBS-induced decrease in firing rate (ZD n = 6, change in firing rate: −22.9 ± 8.6%, p=0.63 vs TBS, Figure 6C–E)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Intracellular ZD7288 did not prevent TBS-induced decrease in input resistance (ZD change in Rin: −14.3 ± 3.8%, p=0.36 vs TBS).
source: decrease in input resistance (ZD change in Rin: −14.3 ± 3.8%, p=0.36 vs TBS, Figure 6F)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Intracellular ZD7288 did not prevent TBS-induced increase in first spike latency (ZD change in latency: 78.7 ± 13.1%, p=0.62 vs TBS).
source: and increase in first spike latency (ZD change in latency: 78.7 ± 13.1%, p=0.62 vs TBS, Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: While plasticity of Ih might have been induced by the stimulation protocol, it would tend to increase rather than decrease intrinsic excitability.
source: These results indicate that while plasticity of Ih might have been induced by our stimulation protocol, it would tend to increase rather than decrease intrinsic excitability.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing increased sag ratio and lack of effect of ZD7288.

claim: Plasticity in another, opposing, mechanism determined the overall change in excitability.
source: Therefore plasticity in another, opposing, mechanism determined the overall change in excitability.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the fact that Ih changes would increase excitability but overall excitability decreased.

claim: ID is a slowly inactivating potassium current activated at subthreshold membrane potentials.
source: The large increases in first spike latency are suggestive of ID, a slowly inactivating potassium current activated at subthreshold membrane potentials (Storm, 1988)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In CA1 pyramidal neurons, ID is carried by Kv1.1 channels expressed at the AIS.
source: which in CA1 pyramidal neurons is carried by Kv1.1 channels expressed at the AIS (Kirizs et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In the presence of DTX-K, the reduction in firing rate was significantly smaller (change in firing rate: TBS −51.8 ± 8.7%, n = 6, DTX-K −25.5 ± 5.3%, n = 6, p=0.037).
source: We found that the reduction in firing rate was significantly smaller with DTX-K (change in firing rate: TBS −51.8 ± 8.7%, n = 6, DTX-K −25.5 ± 5.3%, n = 6, p=0.037, Figure 7C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In the presence of DTX-K, the reduction in input resistance was mostly abolished (change in Rin: TBS −17.4 ± 1.7%, n = 6, DTX-K −5.5 ± 1.7%, n = 6, p=9.7×10−4).
source: the reduction in input resistance was mostly abolished (change in Rin: TBS −17.4 ± 1.7%, n = 6, DTX-K −5.5 ± 1.7%, n = 6, p=9.7×10−4, Figure 7D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In the presence of DTX-K, the increase in latency was mostly abolished (change in latency: TBS 192.0 ± 54.2%, n = 6, DTX-K 51.0 ± 10.8%, n = 6, p=0.04).
source: as was the increase in latency (change in latency: TBS 192.0 ± 54.2%, n = 6, DTX-K 51.0 ± 10.8%, n = 6, p=0.04, Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The reduction in excitability following TBS is mediated, at least in part, by an increase in ID.
source: These results suggest that the reduction in excitability following TBS is mediated, at least in part, by an increase in ID.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that DTX-K attenuated the plasticity.

claim: In the novel condition, the out-of-field firing rate decreased over time (Start 1.58 ± 0.11 Hz, Middle 1.47 ± 0.1 Hz, End 1.37 ± 0.1 Hz, n = 171, F = 5.17 p=0.0065).
source: We found that in the novel condition the out-of-field firing rate decreased over time (Start 1.58 ± 0.11 Hz, Middle 1.47 ± 0.1 Hz, End 1.37 ± 0.1 Hz, n = 171, F = 5.17 p=0.0065, Figure 8A–C)

claim: In the novel condition, the distribution of the lap-by-lap correlation was shifted towards a decrease in activity (n = 171, p=0.0093).
source: and that the distribution of the lap-by-lap correlation was shifted towards a decrease in activity (n = 171, p=0.0093, Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of extracellular recording data with statistical analysis.

claim: The decrease in out-of-field firing rate in the novel condition is compatible with decreased intrinsic excitability.
source: This effect is compatible with decreased intrinsic excitability.

claim: In the novel condition, the in-field firing rate increased across the session (Start 3.63 ± 0.19 Hz, Middle: 3.92 ± 0.21 Hz, End 4.19 ± 0.22 Hz, n = 171, F = 5.02, p=0.0071).

claim: In the familiar condition, no change was detected in the out-of-field firing rate (Start 1.71 ± 0.1 Hz, Middle: 1.62 ± 0.1 Hz, End 1.74 ± 0.11 Hz, n = 268, F = 1.53, p=0.22).

source: The in-field firing rate also did not change over time (Start 5.3 ± 0.23 Hz, Middle: 5.34 ± 0.22 Hz, End 5.15 ± 0.22 Hz, n = 268, F = 0.87, p=0.42, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of extracellular recording data with statistical analysis.

claim: In the familiar condition, there was no change in the in-field firing rate correlation distribution (p=0.25, n = 268).
source: and there was no change in the firing rate correlation distribution (p=0.25, n = 268, Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of extracellular recording data with statistical analysis.

claim: The results from place cell analysis are consistent with the presence of an activity-dependent reduction in intrinsic excitability during exploration of a novel environment.
source: Overall, these results are consistent with the presence of an activity-dependent reduction in intrinsic excitability during exploration of a novel environment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of place cell firing patterns.

claim: Short periods of theta-burst firing can induce a global and long-lasting depression of intrinsic excitability in CA1 pyramidal neurons in vivo.
source: Our results show that short periods of theta-burst firing, mimicking the firing of place cells within their place fields (Epsztein et al., 2011; Harvey et al., 2009), can induce a global and long-lasting depression of intrinsic excitability in CA1 pyramidal neurons in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The plasticity was homeostatic as its magnitude correlated with the number of action potentials used during the induction protocol.
source: This plasticity was homeostatic as its magnitude correlated with the number of action potentials used during the induction protocol.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis presented in the results.

source: Its induction required intracellular calcium
evidence: This claim is supported by the BAPTA experiments showing that calcium chelation prevented the plasticity.

source: and its expression was partially blocked by the Kv1.1 blocker DTX-K, implicating ID in the AIS.

claim: The results demonstrate an additional form of plasticity of intrinsic excitability not previously described in CA1 pyramidal neurons in vitro.
source: These observations demonstrate an additional form of plasticity of intrinsic excitability not previously described in CA1 pyramidal neurons in vitro.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison with previous in vitro studies.

source: This lower dendritic input resistance in vivo (Destexhe et al., 2003), however, also limits the ability of dendritic currents to propagate to the soma
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Changes in dendritic currents may have occurred in the distal dendrites but had little to no impact on somatic excitability.
source: and therefore changes may have occurred in the distal dendrites but had little to no impact on somatic excitability.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about possible explanations for the observations.

claim: Ih regulates excitability locally rather than globally under the experimental conditions.
source: In either case our results suggest that Ih regulates excitability locally rather than globally under our conditions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: An increase in ID was contributing to the decrease in excitability, through increasing the delay to the onset of firing.
source: Our results instead suggest that an increase in ID was contributing to the decrease in excitability, through increasing the delay to the onset of firing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results with DTX-K.

claim: Some Kv1 channels are active at the holding membrane potential.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, we also saw a reduction in the change in input resistance by DTX-K, which suggests that some Kv1 channels are active at the holding membrane potential.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed effect of DTX-K on input resistance.

claim: The overlap of the activation and de-inactivation voltage dependencies of ID at around −75 mV could allow for a small, continuous ID.
source: This could be explained by the overlap of the activation and de-inactivation voltage dependencies of ID at around −75 mV (Storm, 1988), approximately the true holding potential in our recordings, which could allow for a small, continuous ID.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on known properties of ID and citations.

claim: The observation of reduced input resistance by DTX-K favors a shift in the activation properties of the channels over membrane insertion as the mechanism of regulation.
source: This observation also favors a shift in the activation properties of the channels over membrane insertion as the mechanism of regulation, as most of those newly inserted channels would remain closed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: ID is primarily carried by Kv1.1 and its expression is highly localized to the AIS in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: In CA1 pyramidal neurons ID is primarily carried by Kv1.1 and its expression is highly localized to the AIS (Kirizs et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Changes in AIS excitability can have a significant influence on the excitability of a neuron without affecting synaptic integration.
source: As this is the site of action potential generation, changes in AIS excitability can have a significant influence on the excitability of a neuron without affecting synaptic integration (Kole and Stuart, 2012; Rama et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The plasticity in AIS excitability distinguishes it from plasticity in dendritic conductances such as Ih and Ia, which primarily regulate the input rather than output of the neuron.
source: Functionally, this distinguishes it from plasticity in dendritic conductances such as Ih and Ia, which primarily regulate the input rather than output of the neuron.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the functional differences between AIS and dendritic conductances.

claim: DTX-K did not completely prevent the reduction in excitability, which might be explained by incomplete block of Kv1.1 channels or the involvement of other Kv1 channel subtypes.
source: That DTX-K did not completely prevent the reduction in excitability might be explained by incomplete block of Kv1.1 channels or the involvement of other Kv1 channel subtypes (Monaghan et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about possible explanations for the incomplete block.

claim: The incomplete prevention of excitability reduction by DTX-K might be explained by plasticity in other conductances such as inwardly rectifying potassium channels.
source: or by plasticity in other conductances such as inwardly rectifying potassium channels (Kim and Johnston, 2015) which are active around the resting membrane potential.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about possible explanations for the incomplete block.

claim: An increase in the tonic GABA current could contribute to the shift in the input-output curve.
source: Another possibility is an increase in the tonic GABA current, for example through a calcium-dependent increase in GABA-A receptors exocytosis such as has been described in cultured hippocampal neurons (Saliba et al., 2012). This increase could contribute to the shift in the input-output curve
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms.

claim: An increase in tonic GABA current should speed up the membrane time constant and therefore decrease the latency to firing, opposite to what was observed.
source: though it should also speed up the membrane time constant and therefore decrease the latency to firing (Wlodarczyk et al., 2013), opposite to what we observed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from known effects of GABA and citations.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity of Kv1 has typically been associated with structural changes over hours or days in response to sustained input.
source: Homeostatic plasticity of Kv1 has typically been associated with structural changes over hours or days in response to sustained input (Kuba et al., 2015; Cudmore et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The plasticity observed is unusual as it occurs rapidly and in response to a relatively small stimulus.
source: and in this sense the plasticity we observed is unusual, as it occurs rapidly and in response to a relatively small stimulus.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison with typical homeostatic plasticity.

claim: A sensitive mechanism for homeostasis may be necessary in CA1 as pyramidal neurons are characterized by their near silence outside of their active fields.
source: Such a sensitive mechanism for homeostasis may be necessary in CA1 as pyramidal neurons are characterized by their near silence outside of their active fields, and therefore homeostatic regulation based on sustained changes in firing rates, as seen in the neocortex, is less relevant under normal conditions.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the functional significance of the observed plasticity.

claim: CA1 pyramidal neurons are embedded in a complex local feed-back inhibitory network.
source: CA1 pyramidal neurons are embedded in a complex local feed-back inhibitory network (Pouille and Scanziani, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: It is possible that the TBS-induced burst firing was sufficient to induce plasticity in recurrently connected interneurons.
source: and it is possible that the TBS-induced burst firing was sufficient to induce plasticity in recurrently connected interneurons.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms.

claim: Theta-burst firing of CA1 pyramidal cell has been shown to induce plasticity at inhibitory synapses in vitro via retrograde endocannabinoid signaling.
source: Indeed, theta-burst firing of CA1 pyramidal cell has been shown to induce plasticity at inhibitory synapses in vitro via retrograde endocannabinoid signaling (Younts et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The plasticity at inhibitory synapses led to a long-term depression at both somatic and dendritic inhibitory synapses and is thus unlikely to account for the decrease in excitability observed.
source: This plasticity, however, led to a long-term depression at both somatic and dendritic inhibitory synapses and is thus unlikely to account for the decrease in excitability we observed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the direction of the plasticity described in the cited study.

claim: Feed-forward synaptic stimulations were shown to induce plasticity of intrinsic excitability in parvalbumin-expressing basket cells through a mGluR-dependent downregulation of Kv1 channels.
source: On the other hand, feed-forward synaptic stimulations (of the Schaffer collaterals) were shown to induce plasticity of intrinsic excitability (in addition to synaptic plasticity) in parvalbumin-expressing basket cells through a mGluR-dependent downregulation of Kv1 channels (Campanac et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: It is unclear if the mGluR-dependent plasticity in interneurons could be engaged via feedback activation.
source: It is unclear, however, if this plasticity could be engaged via feedback activation.
evidence: This claim expresses uncertainty about the applicability of previous findings.

claim: The effect observed was prevented by intracellular BAPTA and therefore calcium-dependent, unlike the mGluR-mediated plasticity.
source: Opposite to this prediction, our effect was prevented by intracellular BAPTA and therefore calcium-dependent, unlike the mGluR-mediated plasticity
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results with BAPTA.

claim: The initial input resistance of CA1 pyramidal cells was increased in the presence of DTX-K, opposite of what would be expected from increased synaptic inhibition.
source: and the initial input resistance of CA1 pyramidal cells was increased in the presence of DTX-K, opposite of what would be expected from increased synaptic inhibition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations with DTX-K.

claim: A contribution of inhibitory plasticity via other mechanisms is difficult to fully rule out in vivo given the paucity of efficient intracellular blockers of GABA-A receptors.
source: Nonetheless, a contribution of inhibitory plasticity via other mechanisms is difficult to fully rule out in vivo given the paucity of efficient intracellular blockers of GABA-A receptors (Atherton et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim acknowledges limitations in ruling out alternative mechanisms.

claim: The differences between the findings and those in vitro may relate to the nature of the different preparations.
source: The differences between our findings and those in vitro may relate to the nature of the different preparations.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about possible explanations for differences.

claim: The in vitro slice preparation offers many advantages to study synaptic and intrinsic plasticity.
source: The in vitro slice preparation offers many advantages to study synaptic and intrinsic plasticity such as the ability to perform long-lasting high-quality recordings, good spatial and temporal control of stimulated fibers and the ease to deliver antagonists of ligand- and voltage-gated channels.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about in vitro preparations.

claim: The in vitro slice preparation remains artificial, with strongly reduced neuronal activity and inoperant neuromodulatory system.
source: Nevertheless, the in vitro slice preparation remains artificial, the neuronal activity is strongly reduced and the neuromodulatory system is inoperant.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about limitations of in vitro preparations.

claim: The slicing procedure itself is traumatic for the neurons, invoking stress responses alongside inevitable damage to the axons and dendrites, which results in cellular changes that could affect the expression of plasticity.
source: The slicing procedure itself is also traumatic for the neurons, invoking stress responses alongside inevitable damage to the axons and dendrites, which results in cellular changes that could affect the expression of plasticity (Taubenfeld et al., 2002; Ho et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recordings in anesthetized rats afford more stability than awake preparations at the expense of being in an unnatural brain state.
source: To balance these problems we recorded in anesthetized rats, which affords more stability than awake preparations at the expense of being in an unnatural brain state.
evidence: This claim explains the rationale for the experimental approach.

claim: The anesthetics used will have directly and indirectly affected neuronal excitability, including via an allosteric potentiation of GABA-A receptors and activation of inwardly rectifying potassium channels.
source: The anesthetics used will have directly and indirectly affected neuronal excitability, including via an allosteric potentiation of GABA-A receptors and activation of inwardly rectifying potassium channels (Möhler et al., 2002; Nagi and Pineyro, 2014; Hein, 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on anesthetic effects.

claim: Under anesthesia, the levels of neuromodulators that regulate synaptic plasticity differ compared to awake states.
source: and under anesthesia the levels of neuromodulators that regulate synaptic plasticity (Palacios-Filardo and Mellor, 2019; Dias et al., 2013) differ compared to awake states.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: These factors may have influenced the plasticity observed, and therefore its significance needs to be confirmed in behaving animals.
source: These factors may have influenced the plasticity we observed, and therefore its significance needs to be confirmed in behaving animals.
evidence: This claim acknowledges limitations and the need for further validation.

claim: Changes in out-of-field firing during exploration of virtual reality environments are consistent with an activity-dependent decrease in intrinsic excitability.
source: We did, however, see changes in out-of-field firing during exploration of virtual reality environments that are consistent with an activity-dependent decrease in intrinsic excitability.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of place cell data.

claim: Although no changes in out-of-field firing rate were detected in the familiar environment, the same tendency towards a decrease was still visible in the firing rate correlations.
source: These effects were present in novel environments, and although we did not detect any changes in the out-of-field firing rate in the familiar environment, the same tendency towards a decrease was still visible in the firing rate correlations.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of place cell data.

claim: It is not known how synaptic strength outside of the place field is affected by exploration and plasticity within the place field itself.
source: One caveat to consider, however, is that it is not known how synaptic strength outside of the place field is affected by exploration and plasticity within the place field itself (Diamantaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim acknowledges a limitation in interpreting the results.

claim: Plasticity of interneuronal activity may have also been involved in the observed changes.
source: And as discussed above, plasticity of interneuronal activity may have also been involved.
evidence: This claim acknowledges alternative explanations.

claim: Despite open questions, the results show that in a novel environment the excitability of place cells tends to decrease on a timescale that is consistent with the plasticity described.
source: Nonetheless, despite these open questions, our results show that in a novel environment the excitability of place cells tends to decrease on a timescale that is consistent with the plasticity we have described.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings from the place cell analysis.

claim: Fast, sensitive homeostatic plasticity of intrinsic excitability could potentially be involved in the regulation of coding in CA1.
source: Fast, sensitive homeostatic plasticity of intrinsic excitability could potentially be involved in the regulation of coding in CA1.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the functional significance.

claim: The population of neurons that encode an environment or experience is only a subset of the population that could potentially do so.
source: Indeed, the population of neurons that encode an environment or experience is only a subset of the population that could potentially do so (Thompson and Best, 1989)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Cells that are active tend to have higher levels of intrinsic excitability.
source: and those cells that are active tend to have higher levels of intrinsic excitability (Pignatelli et al., 2019; Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016; Alme et al., 2014; Rich et al., 2014; Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014; Epsztein et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Studies that have enhanced excitability in a subset of cells by overexpressing CREB have shown that this biases cells to participate in the engram.
source: Furthermore, studies that have enhanced excitability in a subset of cells by overexpressing CREB have shown that this biases cells to participate in the engram (Kim et al., 2014; Sekeres et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The population of active cells is roughly constant in both CA1 and the amygdala, and selection is determined, in part, competitively through inhibition.
source: As the population of active cells is roughly constant in both CA1 and the amygdala it appears that selection is determined, in part, competitively through inhibition, a process which the more excitable cells are most likely to win (Trouche et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: To prevent the network from becoming dominated by the same sets of neurons requires mechanisms to modulate excitability, without interfering with learning already contained within the synapses.
source: To prevent the network from becoming dominated by the same sets of neurons this requires mechanisms to modulate excitability, without interfering with learning already contained within the synapses, for which global forms of plasticity of intrinsic excitability appear ideally suited.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the functional role of the observed plasticity.

claim: The activity-driven decrease in excitability described might contribute to preventing network domination by the same neurons.
source: The activity-driven decrease in excitability we have described might therefore contribute to such a process.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the functional significance.

claim: cFos-labelled engram cells show reduced likelihood to encode a novel environment.
source: In line with this interpretation, it was recently shown that cFos-labelled engram cells show reduced likelihood to encode a novel environment (Tanaka et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: It remains to be determined how the observed changes relate to the CREB-associated increases in excitability that have been associated with learning.
source: It remains to be determined, though, how these changes relate to the CREB-associated increases in excitability that have been associated with learning (Lisman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim acknowledges an open question for future research.

claim: Enhanced excitability by CREB is associated with a decrease in the AHP.
source: Enhanced excitability by CREB is associated with a decrease in the AHP (Lopez de Armentia et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: No change in AHP was seen in the current study.
source: in which we saw no change.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results.

claim: CREB is not activated by action potential firing, but rather requires calcium entry at the synapses.
source: This is unsurprising though, as CREB is not activated by action potential firing, but rather requires calcium entry at the synapses (Deisseroth et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The balance between action potential-driven plasticity and synaptically-driven changes in intrinsic excitability may determine how the cell contributes to coding future experiences.
source: This points towards the wider question of how action potential-driven plasticity interacts with synaptically-driven changes in intrinsic excitability, as the balance between them may determine how the cell contributes to coding future experiences.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about broader implications.

claim: It remains to be determined how intrinsic excitability is modulated following place field activity in behaving animals.
source: In particular, it remains to be determined how intrinsic excitability is modulated following place field activity in behaving animals (Schmidt-Hieber and Nolan, 2017; Debanne et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim acknowledges an open question for future research.

claim: It remains to be determined if intrinsic excitability is affected by the plateau potentials that have been shown to induce place field formation.
source: and if it is affected by the plateau potentials that have been shown to induce place field formation (Bittner et al., 2015; Diamantaki et al., 2018; Bittner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim acknowledges an open question for future research.
